title: Reuse: modules and the standard library
summary: Import ready-made tools from Python's standard library and organise your own code into modules.
license: Original work for Python Intelligence; license to be chosen by the owner

steps.title: Don't rebuild what already exists
steps.body:
Square roots, averages, random numbers, counting things, dates: you could write all of these yourself,
but Python already ships with well-tested versions in its **standard library**. Using them is a
single `import` away. The same mechanism lets you split your own growing program into files.

steps.title: A module is a named toolbox
steps.body:
A **module** is a named toolbox: a collection of functions, values and classes you can reuse. Some
modules are files of Python code (your own `.py` files are modules too); others, like `math`, are
built into the interpreter. `import math` gives you one name, `math`, through which you reach its
tools: `math.sqrt`, `math.pi`. Keeping each toolbox behind its own name means two modules can both
have a function called `load` without clashing.

questions: Why might `math.sqrt(x)` be clearer to a reader than just `sqrt(x)`?
If two modules both define `load`, how does importing them as modules avoid confusion?

steps.title: Watch an import and a module call
steps.body: `import` binds one new name; the tools are reached through it.

frames.note: `import math` loads the module and binds the name `math` to it.
`math.sqrt` looks up `sqrt` inside the module: the square root of 25 is 5.0.

steps.title: The precise rules
steps.body:
```python
import statistics                 # use as statistics.mean(...)
from collections import Counter   # use as Counter(...) directly
import random as rnd              # an alias: rnd.randint(...)
```

1. A module is loaded the **first** time it is imported in a program (for a `.py` module, its top-level
   code runs then); later imports reuse the loaded module.
2. `import m` adds the single name `m`; `from m import a, b` adds `a` and `b` themselves.
3. Your own `.py` file is a module too: other files can import its functions.
4. Every module has a `__name__`. It is `"__main__"` when the file is run directly, so
   `if __name__ == "__main__":` marks code that should run only as a script, not on import.
5. The standard library is large: `math`, `random`, `statistics`, `collections`, `datetime`, `json`
   and many more are always available.

steps.title: Run it: a quick standard-library tour
steps.body: Predict each line. Seeding `random` makes its numbers repeatable.
steps.code:
import statistics
from collections import Counter
import random as rnd

scores = [72, 90, 85, 90, 64]
print(statistics.mean(scores), statistics.median(scores))
print(Counter(scores).most_common(1))
rnd.seed(7)
print(rnd.randint(1, 6) in range(1, 7))
print(__name__)

steps.title: Your turn: average word length
steps.body:
Complete `average_word_length(text)` using `statistics.mean` on the **lengths** of the words, rounded
to 2 decimal places. Return `0.0` when the text has no words (`mean` of an empty list is an error).
hints: `mean` needs numbers. Build a list of `len(w)` for each word first.
Check `if not words: return 0.0` before calling `mean`, and wrap the result in `round(..., 2)`.

tests.name: simple
tests.code: assert average_word_length('a bb ccc') == 2.0, f"got {average_word_length('a bb ccc')!r}"

tests.name: rounded
tests.code: assert average_word_length('to be or not') == 2.25, f"got {average_word_length('to be or not')!r}"

tests.name: rounds repeating decimals
tests.code: assert average_word_length('a bb bb') == 1.67, f"got {average_word_length('a bb bb')!r}; round to 2 decimal places"

steps.title: Challenge: the most common letters
steps.body:
Write `top_letters(text, n)` that returns a list of the `n` most common **letters** in `text`, ignoring
case and anything that isn't a letter, most common first. Use `collections.Counter` and its
`most_common(n)` method, which returns `(item, count)` pairs.
hints: Build the letters first: `[ch.lower() for ch in text if ch.isalpha()]`.
`Counter(letters).most_common(n)` gives pairs; keep only the letter from each pair.

from collections import Counter

def top_letters(text, n):
    letters = [ch.lower() for ch in text if ch.isalpha()]
    return [letter for letter, count in Counter(letters).most_common(n)]
steps.solution:
from collections import Counter

def top_letters(text, n):
    letters = [ch.lower() for ch in text if ch.isalpha()]
    return [letter for letter, count in Counter(letters).most_common(n)]

questions.prompt: After `from math import sqrt`, how do you call it?
questions.explanation: `from ... import` binds the name `sqrt` itself; the name `math` is not created.

questions.prompt: After `import math as m`, which works?
questions.explanation: The module is bound only to the alias `m`.

questions.prompt: What is `__name__` inside a file you run directly?
questions.explanation: Running a file directly sets its `__name__` to `"__main__"`; when imported, it is the module's name.

questions.prompt: A module is imported in three places in one program. How many times does its top-level code run?
questions.explanation: The first import runs it; later imports reuse the already-loaded module.

steps.title: What you can do now
steps.body:
- Import modules three ways: `import m`, `from m import name`, `import m as alias`.
- Reach for the standard library (`math`, `statistics`, `collections`, `random`) before writing your own.
- Explain why `if __name__ == "__main__":` separates script code from importable code.
